title: C++ in a nutshell
description: What kind of language C++ is, how a program is compiled and linked, and why there is no garbage collector.

content.title: A language close to the machine
content.body:
C++ was created by Bjarne Stroustrup, starting in 1979 as "C with Classes" and renamed C++ in 1983. It adds classes, templates, exceptions and much more to the C language.

A C++ program is compiled directly into native machine code for one processor and one operating system. There is no virtual machine and no garbage collector: the program runs straight on the hardware, and memory is released by the code itself.

Its motto is "you don't pay for what you don't use": a feature you do not use costs nothing at run time. That is why C++ powers games, browsers, databases and embedded systems.

The language is standardized by ISO: C++11 started "modern C++", followed by C++14, 17, 20 and 23.

content.question: You compile main.cpp with g++. What do you get?

choices.text: Native machine code: an executable for your processor and operating system
Bytecode for a virtual machine
Intermediate Language for .NET
JavaScript that runs in the browser

content.explanation: C++ compiles ahead of time to machine code. Nothing needs to be installed to run the executable, unlike Java (JVM) or C# (.NET runtime).

content.question: You built a C++ program on Linux. Can you run the same executable on Windows?

choices.text: No: machine code targets one system; you compile the source code again for Windows
Yes: C++ executables run everywhere
Yes, as long as Java is installed
Only if the program has no classes

content.explanation: The source code can be portable, but the executable is not: it contains machine code and system calls for one platform. Portability comes from recompiling.

content.question: Who releases the memory of the objects a C++ program creates?

choices.text: The program itself: local objects when they go out of scope, heap objects when they are deleted
A garbage collector that runs in the background
The operating system, every few seconds
Nobody: memory is only released when the computer restarts

content.explanation: C++ has no garbage collector. Memory is released at precise moments, when objects are destroyed. The last activity of this course shows how modern C++ makes that automatic.

content.title: Compiling and linking
content.body:
Building a C++ program has several steps:
1. The preprocessor handles the lines starting with #, such as #include <iostream>, which pastes the content of a header file into the code.
2. The compiler turns each .cpp file separately into an object file (.o or .obj).
3. The linker combines the object files and the libraries into one executable.

Headers (.h or .hpp) usually declare functions and classes; .cpp files define them. The program starts in the main() function.

content.question:
#include <iostream>

What does this line do?

choices.text: Before compiling, the preprocessor pastes in the iostream header, which declares std::cout
It downloads the iostream library from the Internet
It loads a module while the program runs
It makes iostream the name of the program

content.explanation: #include is simple text inclusion, done by the preprocessor before the compiler sees the code. C++20 adds modules (import) as a modern alternative.

choices.text: At link time: "undefined reference to add"
When compiling main.cpp
When the program runs and calls add
Never: add returns 0 by default

content.explanation: The declaration is enough to compile main.cpp. It is the linker that looks for the definition of add in all the object files, and fails because there is none.

content.question: Which statements are true?

choices.text: Much C code is also valid C++
C++ adds classes, templates and exceptions to C
C++ is an interpreted language
C++ programs need a garbage collector to run

content.explanation: C++ grew out of C and stays largely compatible with it, but it is compiled, not interpreted, and it has no garbage collector.

content.instructions: Match each part of the build with its role.

pairs.definition: Handles #include and the other # lines before compiling
Turns one .cpp file into an object file
Combines the object files and libraries into an executable
Declares functions and classes to share between .cpp files
The compiled machine code of one .cpp file, not yet runnable
The function where the program starts
